title: Quiz: Mining Rules from the Health Insurance Dataset

questions.text: To convert a data frame of binary (0/1) insurance flag columns into an arules transactions object, which function do you use?
options: as(df, "matrix")
as(df, "transactions")
transactions(df)
arules::read.transactions(df)
questions.explanation: as(df, "transactions") coerces a data frame of logical (or 0/1) columns into an arules transactions object. The columns become items and the rows become transactions.

options: Rules must have at least 2 items total (antecedent + consequent)
Rules must have at least 2 items in the antecedent
The minimum support is divided by 2
Only 2-itemset rules are returned (no longer rules)
questions.explanation: minlen = 2 sets the minimum total number of items in a rule (antecedent ∪ consequent). This filters out trivial single-item 'rules' like {} → {dental_cover} that have no antecedent.

questions.text: In the arulesViz scatter plot (method = 'scatter', shading = 'lift'), what do rules in the TOP-RIGHT corner of the plot represent?
options: Rules with high lift but low confidence
Rules with high support but low confidence
Rules with high support AND high confidence
Rules with low support and low confidence
questions.explanation: The x-axis is support and the y-axis is confidence. The top-right corner therefore contains rules that are both common (high support = they apply to many policyholders) and reliable (high confidence = the consequent is usually present when the antecedent is).

questions.text: You find the rule {vision_cover} → {dental_cover} with confidence = 0.74 and lift = 1.9. Which statement is most accurate?
options: 74% of all policyholders hold dental cover
74% of policyholders with vision cover also hold dental cover, and this is 1.9× the base rate for dental
The rule applies to 74% of all transactions in the dataset
Vision cover causes policyholders to buy dental cover
questions.explanation: Confidence = P(dental | vision) = 0.74 means 74% of vision holders also hold dental. Lift = 1.9 means they are 1.9× more likely to hold dental than a randomly chosen policyholder. Association rules describe co-occurrence, not causation.

questions.text: A high-lift association rule always implies a causal relationship between the antecedent and the consequent.
questions.explanation: Association rules measure co-occurrence, not causation. A high lift means the items appear together more often than chance predicts, but this could be due to a common confounding variable (e.g., both are more common among Gold-tier policyholders) rather than a direct causal link.

questions.text: You want to identify rules where dental_cover is the OUTCOME (consequent). Which arules code achieves this?
options: subset(rules, lhs %in% "dental_cover=TRUE")
subset(rules, rhs %in% "dental_cover=TRUE")
filter(rules, consequent == "dental_cover")
inspect(rules, side = "rhs", item = "dental_cover")
questions.explanation: In arules, rhs refers to the right-hand side (consequent) of the rule. subset(rules, rhs %in% "dental_cover=TRUE") selects only rules where dental_cover=TRUE appears as the outcome, allowing you to study what predicts dental cover uptake.
